broke: a source module named tests.py sits inside the package, so any tool that reads the word tests in a filename will treat the template language's own test functions as a test suite
detail: found by widening rabadon's own discovery and watching it lock two jinja files that are not tests: src/jinja2/tests.py, which implements the is-defined family the template language exposes, and examples/basic/test.py, which is a demo script. not a defect in jinja; a naming collision that any locking tool has to survive, and the reason rabadon now requires a convention rather than a single filename.

broke: the benchmarks page named native/gate_bench.sh as the source of 42.0us to judge one command, and that file did not exist
detail: no micro benchmark existed in the repository at all. the only real measurement was native/bench.py, which times the whole hook and answers a different question. the first honest measurement of judge_command came back 125.5us, three times the number the page had been carrying.

broke: the nine cheat families had never been run against the shipped binary, only against a shell reproduction of the arbiter
detail: the audit's sentence 'REPAIR_OK plus VERIFIED would have been printed' rested on cheats/arena.sh, not on rabadon-repair. run end to end with each corpus proposer in RABADON_CLAUDE_BIN against the corpus's own pristine-red checkouts: 10 families, 10 refused, 0 accepted, 0 held patches carrying the defect. two by the test lock, four by the harness lock, two by the held-out probe, one by the check staying red. the first pass through this runner is what surfaced the truncation bug above.

broke: the gate's Bash decision site was a hand-written second copy of rbrules::judge_command, the exact caller rules.h warns about
detail: rules.h says a caller who re-implements half of judge_command is how exec became a bypass, and the caller doing it was the gate itself. the two answers agreed and nothing held them there. the gate calls the shared verdict now, and gate_bench.sh replays all 34 fixture cases through both and refuses to print a timing unless every verdict matches.

broke: the overview kept its headline numbers by hand and had drifted 31 refusals and 39 commits behind the pages generated from the same sources
detail: the catches page rebuilds itself from the gate spool and the patch-notes page from git log; the overview did not, so it started lying the moment the next command was refused. it is a template now and the test refuses any literal in a headline slot.

broke: the overview showed 100.0% precision as a headline while the same binary replayed against this machine's real ledger read 26.3%, and the repo already carried both numbers
detail: the fixture is 34 cases lifted out of real sessions and it is not wrong, it is narrow. replayed against all 215 real refusals in the spool the gate still stops 15 real dangers and lets 0 through, but it also cuts 42 pieces of legitimate work, 41 of which are rabadon's own red-team labs. excluding those it reads 93.8%. all three are on the page now with the command for each, next to the 58 of 95 named escapes still open. a product whose pitch is prove-do-not-claim cannot show the flattering number alone.

broke: a notes file naming three unreleased projects was committed and pushed to the public repository
detail: site/build.py already states the rule it broke: names of unreleased projects do not go on a public page. sanitised at HEAD. the names remain in the history of one commit and taking them out needs a history rewrite and a force push, which is the operator's call and was not taken.

broke: the install suite proved the published path on a machine that has a compiler, so it could not tell a prebuilt binary from one compiled during postinstall
detail: the package ships a postinstall that builds from source with clang++ or g++ when no platform package matches, and the README promises a prebuilt binary to someone who has neither. section 6 installs into a second clean prefix with cc, gcc, g++, clang, clang++, c++, make, cmake and ld replaced by shims that log and exit 127. install succeeds, the shim log is empty, and rabadon --version prints 0.2.0 from a real Mach-O binary out of the tarball.

broke: the public site was a Vercel login wall: rabadon.noseydewdrop.com answered 302 to an SSO redirect, and the only reachable URL served the previous hand-written page
detail: site/ had been linked to a second Vercel project named after its own directory, while the custom domain belongs to the rabadon project. aliasing a domain onto another project's deployment leaves deployment protection in force, so every visitor got the login screen and 200 only ever came back from rabadon.vercel.app, which was still serving 207 refusals and 42.0us. relinked to the rabadon project; the domain answers 200 with the generated page.

broke: rabadon --version answered: unknown command "--version", which is the first thing anybody runs after an install
detail: every native binary underneath answers --version and the one command a user actually types did not. found by installing the tarball into a prefix where every compiler on PATH was replaced by a shim that logs its own name and exits 127. the verb asks the BINARY rather than carrying a version string, so the script cannot report a version the installed core does not have.

broke: the hash lock silently locked nothing on any suite big enough to matter: repair read rabadon-truth's JSON out of a buffer that keeps only the last 4000 bytes
detail: measured on the corpus commander checkout: truth discovers 122 test files in 4503 bytes and repair locked 0 of them, while express fit in 2382 bytes and locked all 91. the bigger the suite the less of it was protected. the cost is in the suite's third case: on a 161-file suite a proposer that rewrote the failing test to assert True was HELD instead of rejected. the truth call now keeps its whole answer, and a JSON that cannot be read at all says so instead of passing for a repo with no tests.

broke: the HELD, UNVERIFIED headline stopped naming which half of the proof was missing when the harness-lock work rewrote it
detail: the word anti-tamper fell out of the sentence, so the screen withheld the word VERIFIED without saying why the tamper check had not run. repair_session_test.sh had been red on exactly this line and make test was failing on it.

broke: three silent bounds in test discovery meant whole suites were never locked: a depth limit of 4, patterns that never matched a file named exactly test.ts, and a 512-file list cap
detail: the corpus counted what discovery found against what is on disk: zod 170 test files, 2 discovered, because its suite sits at packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests and the walk turned around at depth 4. date-fns 253 on disk, 16 discovered, none of them a real test, because every one of its files is called test.ts and sits beside the function it tests. depth is 12 now, the list cap 4096, the walk budget 200000, and all three announce themselves in discoveryCapped so repair can say the lock covers less than the suite. the twin came from a real repo and narrowed the rule: jinja has one examples/basic/test.py and a src/jinja2/tests.py that is source, and the first pass locked both, so a bare test stem now counts only where the repo repeats it across three directories.
